body_markdown:
I’ve spent much of my career working in technology, but I know surprisingly little about what happens inside a factory: How does a production line actually work? How do machines know what to do? And how much human involvement does it take to manufacture the products we use every day?


These were some of the questions I brought to Smart Production Solutions (SPS) 2026 in Nuremberg, Germany.


As I attended presentations and explored the show floor, I wanted to understand where industrial automation is heading. I learned quite a bit about how things get made, including something as ordinary as a bottle of household cleaner from P&G. I had never really thought about how much engineering goes into making something I routinely pick up at the supermarket.


I also began to understand how AI and software are changing manufacturing. A few things stayed with me.


### **Industrial AI Is Getting Closer To The Production Process**


I spend a lot of time thinking about AI, mostly from an enterprise technology perspective. Manufacturing gave me a different way of looking at it. Take quality inspection: On a production line, bottles of household cleaner pass through various stages before they’re ready to ship. Checking that every bottle meets quality requirements is an important part of that process. What interested me was what could happen once the system detects a defect. Could AI help identify the cause? Could it suggest an adjustment to the production process? Eventually, could the system make certain corrections itself? AI-enabled visual inspection already allows manufacturers to examine products as they move along the line and identify defects that might otherwise escape detection. The next step is understanding how AI could help manufacturers respond to those defects.


I had always associated industrial automation with machines following programmed instructions. Now I am beginning to see how[physical AI](https://www.forrester.com/report/physical-ai-perceives-reasons-and-acts-in-the-real-world/RES193925?ref_search=4908833_1795768055656) could enable those systems to respond more intelligently to what actually happens during production.


### **Software-Defined Automation Sounds Familiar, Until You Put It In A Factory**


Another topic that caught my attention was[software-defined automation](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-software-defined-factory-holds-the-key-to-adaptable-manufacturing/RES182190?ref_search=4908833_1795768138351) . Industrial automation has traditionally relied on specialized hardware and the software that controls it. Making changes to production equipment can require considerable engineering effort. Software-defined automation aims to reduce the dependency on specific hardware by shifting more automation functions into software. Coming from IT, I recognized the thinking immediately. We have spent years separating software from hardware, making systems easier to update and giving developers more flexibility to test changes before deploying them. Applying similar principles to manufacturing could make it easier to modify production processes or introduce new capabilities.


But I also realized how different the environment is. A software update in an office application is one thing. Changing software that controls physical machinery is quite another. That difference helped me understand why industrial automation follows a different path from enterprise IT, even when both share similar technology concepts.


### **Could Factories Eventually Run Without People?**


This was probably the question that stayed with me longest. During one discussion, I heard about a production environment where machines had operated for several hours during a night shift without anyone on site to supervise them — I found that remarkable. We’re accustomed to thinking about automated production lines. But a factory that can monitor its own operations, recognize problems, and make certain adjustments without someone constantly watching is a different proposition. Of course, running unattended for a few hours is very different from operating an entire factory autonomously.


There are also practical questions. What happens when something unexpected occurs? How much decision-making can we safely entrust to machines? And what does this mean for the people who currently operate and maintain production equipment? I suspect we’ll see more examples of factories operating with less direct human intervention. But I would hesitate to conclude that fully autonomous factories are just around the corner.


### **What I Took Away**


I went to SPS knowing very little about industrial automation. I came away with a better understanding of how manufacturing works and a growing curiosity about where it is heading. What surprised me was how familiar some of the technology discussions sounded. Software-defined architectures and AI are topics I have followed for years. But seeing these technologies at work in physical production gave me a different perspective.


I also gained a new appreciation for the complexity behind everyday products. I doubt I will look at a bottle of household cleaner quite the same way again.


And I keep coming back to one question: If factories can increasingly recognize problems and adjust their own operations, how much human involvement will they eventually need? I don’t know the answer. But after SPS, I certainly want to learn more.
